sents.text: Say who: u for the user who owns it, g for group, o for others, a for all.
Then plus to add, or minus to remove.
chmod u plus x train dot sh lets you run your script.
chmod o minus r secrets dot txt stops everyone else from reading it.
You'll often see permissions as numbers.
Read is four, write is two, execute is one, and you add them up.
Seven is read, write and execute; six is read and write; five is read and execute; four is read only.
Three digits mean owner, group and others.
So seven five five is the usual setting for programs and folders, six four four for normal files, and six hundred for private files, like keys.
You write a script, try to run it with dot slash train dot sh, and get permission denied: the file isn't marked as executable yet.
chmod u plus x, run it again, and it works.
The dot slash just means: the file in this folder.
chown changes the owner and the group: user, colon, group.
Only the administrator can give files away, so chown usually needs sudo, which is next lesson's topic.
You'll meet chown when files created by one program have to be used by another.
